podcast.title: Chart Popularity in 1962 (1962)
podcast.body: In 1962, instrumentals were highly popular on the charts, with "vocal-less hits" such as "Stranger on the Shore," "The Stripper," and "Telstar" all reaching number one. "Instrumentals were hot on the charts in 62 to more vocal less hits called the stripper and tell star went to number one that year."

podcast.title: "Mood Music" for Older Audiences
podcast.body: Instrumental albums were a common category stocked in early record stores and general retailers. These records were often marketed as "moon music" or mood music, specifically targeting older demographics. "Plenty of those instrumental albums that were supposed to be good for moon music for older people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Challenges in Mainstream Exposure
podcast.body: Prior to the PBS pledge drive phenomenon, instrumental music, especially in the new age genre, faced significant hurdles in gaining mainstream exposure. It was generally not considered "radio friendly," and platforms like MTV made "not a lot of room for instrumental new age composers," pushing artists to find alternative avenues for their work. "An MTV wasn't exactly making a lot of room for instrumental new age composers."

podcast.title: Continued Relevance in Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Despite the shift towards vocal music, purely instrumental rock and roll hits continued to appear into the 1960s, and instrumental groups like The Ventures and The Shadows were fundamental to the existence of rock and roll guitar bands. "But while into the 1960s we'll still be seeing rock and roll hits that were purely instrumental. Indeed we probably wouldn't have rock and roll guitar bands at all, without instrumental groups like the Ventures in the US, or the Shadows in the UK, who had hits with pure instrumental records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dominance for Dancing (1920s-1950s)
podcast.body: For much of the period from the 1920s through the early 1950s, instrumental groups were the preferred choice for dance music, with big bands led by instrumentalists rather than vocalists. "for most of the decades from the 1920s, through to the early 50s, if you wanted music for dancing, you would want instrumental groups."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Shift to Vocal Dominance
podcast.body: The music industry transitioned from being dominated by instrumental music to being dominated by singers primarily out of necessity, following the musician's union strikes of the 1940s. "It was only with the musician's union strikes of the 1940s, which we've talked about before, that more food necessity than anything else. The music industry moved from being dominated by instrumental music to being dominated by singers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
